text: Which of the following snippets correctly define a function? (Select two answers.)

options.text:
def 0_effects(parameter):
    return parameter + 0

def no_operation(parameter):
    return parameter

def do_not_touch:
    parameter *= 1

explanation_en: def 0_effects(parameter): The function name is incorrect – it must not begin with a digit. def do_not_touch: The declaration is erroneous – it lacks a pair of parentheses right after the function name. The other two snippets are correct function definitions.

text: A user-defined function is invoked twice in the following line of code. What do you call the argument passing techniques which have been used here? (Select two answers.)

options.text: keyword
positional
reference
indicatory

explanation_en: keyword: the inner invocation (the one with the phrase parameter=0) makes use of this technique. positional: the outer function invocation uses this technique. reference: there is no such phenomenon in Python as reference parameter passing. indicatory: we don't have any idea what this term would mean – do you?

text: Which of the following functions cannot be invoked with one argument?

options.text:
def four():
    pass

def three(level, size = 0):
    pass

def two(level):
    pass

def one(level=100):
    pass

explanation_en: def four(): The only number of arguments this function can accept is zero – this can be deduced from the meaningful emptiness between the parentheses. def three(level, size = 0): The function can be invoked with either one or two arguments. def two(level): The function can be invoked with one argument only. def one(level=100): the function can be invoked with zero or one argument.

text: Which of the following functions can be invoked with one argument?

options.text:
def one(zeroes=0):
    pass

def four():
    pass

def two(first, second):
    pass

def three(vertex_1, vertex_2, vertex_3 = 0):
    pass

explanation_en: def one(zeroes=0): Yes, it can. Moreover, it can be invoked without any arguments – the default parameter value will be used then. def four(): You are not allowed to pass arguments to this function. def two(first, second): This function demands two arguments and this is an indisputable requirement. def three(vertex_1, vertex_2, vertex_3 = 0): This function needs either two or three arguments.

text: What is the expected result of running the following code?
code:
def process(data):
    data = [1, 2, 3]
    return data[-2]


measurements = [0 for i in range(3)]
process(measurements)
print(measurements[-2])

options.text: The code raises an unhandled exception.
The code prints 1.
The code prints 0.
The code prints 2.

explanation_en: Note: the process() function redefines (reassigns) its parameters, which means that the parameter visible locally (in the function's scope) refers to different data than the argument used globally. It also means that this change doesn't affect global data. Therefore the measurements list still contains zeros.

text: What is the expected result of running the following code?
code:
def process(data):
    data[1] = 2
    return data[-2]


measurements = [0 for i in range(3)]
process(measurements)
print(measurements[-2])

options.text: The code prints 1.
The code prints 2.
The code raises an unhandled exception.
The code prints 0.

explanation_en: Note: the process() function redefines (reassigns) the second element of its parameter, which means that the change affects the argument (which is visible globally). This is why the middle element of the measurements list (which can be indexed as [-2]) contains 2, not zero.

text: What is the expected output of the following code?
explanation_en: As walk() is a recursive function, we need to trace all its invocations. Note that the function returns the sum of its argument and the result returns by itself. 1. walk(2) which returns 2 + walk(1). 2. walk(1) which returns 1 + walk(0). 3. walk(0) which returns 0 and breaks the invocation chain. 4. consequently, the final result is 2 + 1 + 0.

text: What is true about exceptions in Python? (Select two answers.)

options.text: IndexError may be raised when you try to access a nonexistent list element.
Slicing a list can raise an exception.
An unhandled exception causes the program to terminate.
IndexError may be raised when you try to access a nonexistent dictionary key.

explanation_en: IndexError may be raised when you try to access a nonexistent list element – True: this is what the exception is intended for. Slicing a list can raise an exception – False: even the craziest slicing is not able to induce an exception. If all slice indices are integers, nothing bad will happen. An unhandled exception causes the program to terminate – True: you've experienced this many times, haven't you? IndexError for a nonexistent dictionary key – False: this kind of problem is served by the KeyError exception.

text: What is false about exceptions in Python? (Select two answers.)

options.text: If any of the raised exceptions remains unhandled, program execution is terminated and an error message is printed.
Any code put inside the try branch is always fully executed.
More than one except branch can be executed when an exception is raised.
The code put inside the try branch may not be fully executed.

explanation_en: If any of the raised exceptions remains unhandled… – True: you've experienced this many times, haven't you? Any code put inside the try branch is always fully executed – Wrong: the code can be broken and left when an error occurs. More than one except branch can be executed when an exception is raised – Wrong: not more than one except branch is executed in case of error. The code put inside the try branch may not be fully executed – Absolutely.
